crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Self-Driving Laboratories
children.blurb: Self-driving laboratories are experimental platforms that combine automated hardware, sensors, and machine learning to plan, execute, and interpret experiments with limited human intervention.

children.name: Digital Twins for Experiments
children.blurb: A digital twin for an experiment is a live computational model of a physical laboratory setup, its instruments, samples, and protocols, used to plan, monitor, and interpret runs.

children.name: Instrument and Sensor Data
children.blurb: Instrument and sensor data in laboratory automation and simulation covers the raw and processed signals from analytical instruments, environmental sensors, imaging systems, and robotic lab equipment.

children.name: Optimising Lab Protocols
children.blurb: Optimising lab protocols uses AI and simulation to refine the sequence, timing, and parameters of experimental procedures.

children.name: Forecasting Lab Supplies
children.blurb: Forecasting lab supplies means predicting future demand for consumables, reagents, equipment parts, and other inventory in research and clinical laboratories.

sections.body: Laboratory automation and simulation covers the use of artificial intelligence to run physical experiments, model them before they happen, and manage the data and materials around them. Self-driving laboratories combine robotic instruments with machine learning that chooses the next experiment from the results so far. Digital twins are computational copies of an experiment or instrument that let researchers test changes without using reagents or machine time. Instrument and sensor data work involves cleaning, aligning, and interpreting raw output from spectrometers, microscopes, and other devices. Protocol optimisation uses search methods to adjust temperatures, timings, and concentrations for better yield or signal. Forecasting lab supplies predicts consumption of reagents and consumables so that runs do not stop for lack of material.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is real but uneven. Closed loop optimisation works for well defined chemical reactions and simple biological assays where the search space is small and the measurement is fast. Digital twins are reliable for equipment with known physics, such as thermal cycling or fluid flow in simple geometries, but they break down when the underlying model is incomplete. Instrument data pipelines still require custom parsing for many vendor formats and are not yet plug and play. Protocol optimisation can tune a handful of parameters but cannot yet redesign a multi step protocol from scratch. Supply forecasting is accurate for stable, high volume items and weak for rare or bursty demand. The honest limit is that most systems work inside one lab or one instrument class, and transferring them to a new setting usually requires substantial rework.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Self-Driving Laboratories to see the full loop from experiment to model to next experiment. Digital Twins for Experiments explains the simulation layer that often sits beside that loop, letting a researcher test a decision before spending physical resources. Instrument and Sensor Data is the input layer, covering how raw readings become the structured data that both self-driving labs and digital twins depend on. Optimising Lab Protocols sits between the data and the next run, showing how models choose what to change. Forecasting Lab Supplies is the planning layer, concerned with having enough material and capacity for the experiments the other pages describe. Together the five pages move from the physical loop, to the simulated copy, to the data, to the decision, and finally to the resources that make the work possible.
